stories.topic: A Monopoly That Built a Factory for Ideas
stories.summary: Bill Gates once said that with a time machine he would visit Bell Labs in December 1947, when the transistor was created there. Bell Labs was AT&T's research arm, and by the 1960s it employed more than 15,000 people, over 1,200 of them PhDs. Amit traces this to how the business was structured. Telephony was close to a natural monopoly, and AT&T accepted obligations such as serving remote areas. In return it had a guaranteed revenue stream, which let it fund research that did not have to pay off by next quarter. AT&T put only about 2.8% of revenue into R&D, and roughly 0.3% into basic research. But that research could run on very long horizons. Arthur C. Clarke said the New Jersey site looked like a factory, and that it was one: a factory for ideas.
stories.insight: Freedom from short-term pressure mattered more than the size of the budget. Ajay adds that Murray Hill's roughly 3,000 staff and 1,000 PhDs is a scale many organisations, including private players in India, could fund on a twenty-year horizon. So the real secret was culture and management, not money.
stories.quote: But it is a factory for ideas. And so its production lines are invisible.

stories.topic: 'Hey, I'm Dick, Let's Go for Lunch'
stories.summary: In his Unix memoir, Brian Kernighan recalls settling into his new Bell Labs office when a stranger walked in, said 'Hey I'm Dick, let's go for lunch,' and took him out. Only later did Kernighan realise this was the great Richard Hamming, whose textbook he had learned from. Thompson, Ritchie and other greats were just across the hall. No single boss controlled anyone's career, and hierarchies formed around whom people respected. Amit links this to the work-from-home debate and to Shane Parrish's tweet that people who show up at the office end up as bosses of those who work from home. He also notes that about half of Everything is Everything's episodes, including Seven Stories That Should Be Films and the math episode, came about on the fly because the two hosts were in the same room.
stories.insight: Creativity comes from proximity and casual interaction, not from showing up for the sake of it. Kernighan's summary of the point is 'geography is destiny.'
stories.quote: where the real work happens, the real creativity happens is in the watercooler conversations. It's in the beer after the office work.

stories.topic: The Professor Who Forged Ken Thompson's Signature
stories.summary: As an undergraduate at UC Berkeley, Ken Thompson worked on the computer from midnight to 8 a.m., the only hours he could have the whole machine to himself. He called it his personal computer. When a professor asked whether he would apply to graduate school, Thompson said no because he thought he wasn't good enough. Without telling him, the professor filled out the application, forged his signature and sent it in. Thompson was accepted.
stories.insight: That era let teachers judge the person instead of following procedure. A world where admissions run purely on rules would have lost Ken Thompson.
stories.quote: without telling him that professor filled up his application for attending a master's or a PhD, I forget which, and forged his signature and submitted the application form, and the guy was accepted.

stories.topic: How Ajay's Father Got Into a PhD Without the Marks
stories.summary: Ajay's father returned to education late in life. He did his undergraduate degree at night school and then a master's in economics at Bombay University. He was a respected figure there, but his exam marks were poor, and he was gloomy because he assumed a PhD was now out of reach. The senior economists of the department, D.T. Lakdawala, P.R. Brahmananda, M.L. Dantwala and others, talked it over among themselves. They knew him as their student, and they told him they were taking him into the PhD anyway.
stories.insight: Discretion exercised by people who know you can beat cut-offs. Ajay worries that India now turns everything into black-and-white rules and opposes all forms of discretion, and so loses the essence.
stories.quote: actually we should always look at the person and not at mechanical procedure.

stories.summary: Thompson refused Bell Labs at first, saying he would never work for a corporation. They kept after him and flew him east to give a talk. Walking down the corridor and reading the names on the office doors, he thought how amazing it would be to work near those people. After the talk he drove to a friend's house, where a printed offer reached him, and then on to a motel somewhere in New Jersey. Bell Labs called him there to ask whether he had accepted. When he asked how they had found him, they said they had phoned every motel in New Jersey. He accepted.
stories.insight: Talent clusters recruit by being visible: the names on the doors did most of the persuading. And a great organisation uses whatever unusual advantages it actually has.
stories.quote: Well, we're the telephone company. We found the phone number of every motel in New Jersey and we made all the calls and we found you.

stories.topic: Unix in Three Weeks on a Junk PDP-7
stories.summary: After the Multics failure, Bell Labs management refused to fund any more operating-systems research. Thompson found an obsolete PDP-7 that nobody wanted, with about 16 to 32 KB of memory and a disk that was too fast for it. He wrote a Space Travel game on it, then a disk scheduler and a file system to cope with the mismatched disk. At that point he realised he was three weeks from a complete operating system. His wife and child left to visit his parents in California, so he spent one week writing an editor, one week an assembler and one week the kernel. Unix booted. Its name was a play on Multics, signalling something stripped down.
stories.insight: Junk hardware, no funding and a hard deadline produced elegance. Ajay jokes that this is an argument against declutter manifestos: keep your old PDP-7s, because they can amount to something.
stories.quote: he planned it as one week to write an editor, one week to write an assembler, one week to write the operating system kernel, in three weeks I'll be done.

stories.topic: Smuggling an Operating System Inside a Patent Typesetter
stories.summary: Bell Labs filed roughly one patent a day, and each needed strict formatting, diagrams and equations. Management was about to buy a specialised typesetting system from an outside vendor. The Unix team offered to build an internal document-processing system for the same money. Privately they knew the real result would be Unix running on modern hardware. Management agreed. The project produced roff, nroff and troff. Ajay says the 'markup' in HTML (hypertext markup language) originates here: formatting commands embedded inside plain text.
stories.insight: When managers won't fund the bet you believe in, attach it to an adjacent problem they will pay for, and deliver both.
stories.quote: So for the money that management was about to pay somebody for a specialized piece of patent processing software, they were going to write an entire typesetting system, a document processing system, and run it on Unix and build Unix out on some modern hardware.

stories.topic: Inventing C So Unix Could Be Rewritten
stories.summary: At the time, every operating system was written in assembly language, which took someone of Thompson's ability. Dennis Ritchie asked whether Unix could be written in a high-level language instead. None of the existing languages was good enough, so Ritchie and others created C. Thompson and Ritchie then rewrote all of Unix in C, and Unix suddenly became portable to more and more machines.
stories.insight: Sometimes you have to build the tool that lets you build the thing. Ajay calls C, a by-product of that effort, the most important programming language in the world today.
stories.quote: And C was written to make it possible to write Unix in C.

stories.topic: How Antitrust Accidentally Set Unix Free
stories.summary: Unix was far ahead of the competition, and AT&T could have launched its own computers and operating system and become a bigger monopoly. Ajay thinks it held back because it was tied up with the US FTC, and an OS business would have looked like an extension of its telecom monopoly. Instead it licensed Unix, source code included, to universities under academic licences. A famous two-volume work printed the kernel source with a line-by-line commentary, so students everywhere learned how an operating system is built. At Berkeley, Bill Joy connected Unix to computer networking, making it the vehicle of TCP/IP and the internet. Sun Microsystems and others followed.
stories.insight: Regulatory pressure kept AT&T from locking Unix up, and that hesitation helped create the foundations of the open-source world and the modern internet.
stories.quote: I think that there was significant pressure on ATT at the time from the antitrust authorities. And that impeded the ability of ATT to turn this into a product.

stories.summary: In 1991 a young student in Finland, Linus Torvalds, posted on Net News that he had been playing with the Minix code and had written a new operating system. Andy Tanenbaum, an eminent computer scientist, replied with a harsh critique. Ajay, who was a little older than Linus, felt Tanenbaum was being unfair and emailed Linus not to lose heart. Ajay booted Linux at an early version, and apart from seven or eight years on Mac OS X it has been his only system since.
stories.insight: Ajay was present at the start of something that now runs the world, and a few kind words to an unknown newcomer under attack are worth sending.
stories.quote: So I wrote email to Linus saying you should not be disheartened. What you're doing is very important.

stories.topic: The Bell Labs President Defends a Chess Program
stories.summary: During a demo for an important visitor, Ken Thompson showed a chess program he was writing. The visitor asked why anyone would waste time on that. Thompson had built a dynamic-programming solution to the chess endgame: list every mating position and work backwards to find the moves that lead there. Dynamic programming came from Richard Bellman and Robert Kalaba at RAND. Kalaba was Ajay's teacher, and Ajay's own PhD thesis, on women in Malaysia, rested on the idea. Amit notes that endgames with seven or fewer pieces are now solved. The Bell Labs president answered the visitor that the algorithms developed along the way were helping schedule phone calls in the Bell system.
stories.insight: Good research management means shielding playful work from people who demand an immediate use, and seeing how a game connects to the core business.
stories.quote: So the president of Bell Labs understood those connections.

stories.summary: At NeXT, Steve Jobs chose BSD Unix as the base, and when he returned to Apple the NeXT team brought it with them, producing Mac OS X. The people Jobs trusted most had always told him BSD Unix was the path for operating systems, but he was taking that on their word. Then iTunes was written in roughly a week on the Unix environment taking shape inside Apple.
stories.insight: One concrete demonstration can turn borrowed belief into real conviction. That week is part of why Apple's phones and tablets run Unix today.
stories.quote: When iTunes got done in a week, Steve Jobs is said to have got religion.

stories.summary: Nandan Nilekani, Sanjay Jain and others on the Aadhaar project picked out the hardest part of the problem. They had to match one person against about 1.4 billion records to catch fake IDs, authenticate people for things like PDS rations, and remove duplicate entries. They asked the world's top computer companies and research groups to build it, and several came back saying it could not be done. So the team wrote it themselves.
stories.insight: This is the Unix approach applied to public policy: find the hot spot, solve it first, and once the hard pieces are done the rest is ordinary project execution.
stories.quote: And they turn around and they wrote it themselves and they did it.

stories.topic: Hundreds of People Wrote Our Book
stories.summary: Ajay admires how Bell Labs researchers gave their time freely to review each other's drafts and improve each other's writing. He says the same is true of his own book with Vijay Kelkar. It looks like the work of two authors, but a whole community supplied ideas, argued with them, read drafts and made basic improvements to the table of contents.
stories.insight: Serious work is collective. Helping others with their books and projects is something we owe each other, and nobody is big enough to write a book alone.
stories.quote: I have a book co-authored with Kelkar where it looks like Kelkar and I did it. Actually hundreds of people did it.

stories.topic: The Show's Own Audience, Crunched in One Line of Awk
stories.summary: In his screencast, Ajay runs a one-line awk command on the show's monthly viewing data. In June 2023 the show delivered about 300 hours to 1,947 unique viewers, roughly 9 minutes each, which he reads as mostly curious onlookers. By November about 14,000 unique viewers averaged around 45 minutes. He attributes the rise to the early information asymmetry fading as a loyal audience formed.
stories.insight: A few minutes on the command line can answer a real business question, and anyone who does this has quietly become a programmer.
stories.quote: this minutes per unique viewer has risen through these first six months of the show from 9 minutes to 45 minutes.

recommendations.item: The Idea Factory: Bell Labs and the Great Age of American Innovation
recommendations.creator: Jon Gertner
recommendations.context: Amit's 'first recommendation of today', given while explaining Bell Labs. The title comes from Arthur C. Clarke's description of the place.
recommendations.reason: It explains how Bell Labs' long-horizon culture made it a factory of ideas whose output became the foundation of the modern world.

recommendations.item: UNIX: A History and a Memoir
recommendations.creator: Brian Kernighan
recommendations.context: Amit drew on it for the Hamming lunch story and the 'geography is destiny' line, and called it a must read.
recommendations.reason: An insider's account of how Bell Labs' collegial, boss-less culture and physical closeness produced Unix.

recommendations.item: UNIX: A History and a Memoir
recommendations.creator: Brian Kernighan
recommendations.context: Third of Ajay's closing recommendations.
recommendations.reason: A short history of the early years of Unix and Bell Labs, written by someone who was there.

recommendations.item: Numerical Methods for Scientists and Engineers
recommendations.creator: Richard Hamming
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes. It is the Hamming textbook Kernighan had learned from before Hamming casually invited him to lunch.
recommendations.reason: A route into the work of the Bell Labs great behind 'the purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.'

recommendations.item: A Commentary on the UNIX Operating System
recommendations.creator: John Lions
recommendations.context: Ajay's 'famous book': one volume prints the Unix kernel source, the other explains it line by line.
recommendations.reason: It let universities around the world see how a real operating system is written, which made Unix the lingua franca of a generation of computer scientists.

recommendations.creator: William Strunk and EB White
recommendations.context: Mentioned as the model for Kernighan's programming-style book.
recommendations.reason: It teaches the values of good prose: simplicity, elegance, being easy to understand, no word out of place.

recommendations.creator: Brian Kernighan and PJ Plauger
recommendations.context: Raised in Amit's question about elegance. Ajay cites its link to Strunk and White as proof that culture and engineering belong together.
recommendations.reason: It applies the virtues of clear prose to code and shows that writing well and programming well are the same discipline.

recommendations.creator: Don Norman
recommendations.context: Given by Amit as 'a really quick mid-episode recommendation'.
recommendations.reason: It teaches that anything beautiful is also beautifully functional, otherwise it isn't beautiful, and the same holds for engineering.

recommendations.item: In the Beginning...Was the Command Line
recommendations.creator: Neal Stephenson
recommendations.context: First of Ajay's closing recommendations.
recommendations.reason: It isn't an engineering book. Ajay says Stephenson, a great novelist, understands this world deeply and conveys its dream and philosophy with instinct and passion.

recommendations.creator: Eric S Raymond
recommendations.context: Second of Ajay's closing recommendations.
recommendations.reason: It contrasts the cathedral, where a few great people build in one place, with the bazaar, where thousands argue in public. Ajay credits Raymond as the first to grasp why the unpaid, open bazaar produces the world's best software.

recommendations.context: A credit-card-sized Linux computer costing roughly 2,000 to 5,000 rupees, plus whatever you add, such as a keyboard, a temperature sensor or a plant-watering controller.
recommendations.reason: Ajay says everyone should play with one: it's cheap, it boots Linux, it's a delight to tinker with, and people even use it to build art installations. The show notes call it the best bang for the buck.

recommendations.item: A home router that runs an open-source Unix
recommendations.context: Mentioned while describing how Unix is everywhere, including in routers.
recommendations.reason: You can tinker with the software that runs your own network equipment.

recommendations.creator: Linus Torvalds
recommendations.context: How 10,000 to 20,000 programmers around the world, including some in India, collaborate on the Linux kernel in the open.
recommendations.reason: Anyone, anywhere can watch world-class developers work and join in, starting with bug reports or documentation and moving up to code. Ajay calls this miraculously empowering for places far from Bell Labs.

recommendations.context: Used in the screencast to convert his org file of episode ideas into a Word document for Amit, then wrapped in a homemade command.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's 'Swiss army knife': it converts between almost any document formats from the command line, so you can automate tasks you repeat.

recommendations.context: Ajay keeps his future-episode ideas in it. He contrasts it with Roam Research, the cloud tool he shares with Amit.
recommendations.reason: Hierarchical notes that fold and expand, stored as a plain-text file on your own machine that any Unix tool can search and manipulate.

recommendations.context: The list of the world's 500 most powerful computers.
recommendations.reason: Evidence that Unix won: about 490 or more of them run some variant of Unix.

recommendations.item: Shane Parrish's tweet on working from home
recommendations.creator: Shane Parrish
recommendations.context: Cited in the discussion of Bell Labs' 'geography is destiny' culture.
recommendations.reason: Its point is that people who come into the office end up as bosses of those who work from home. Amit's reason isn't presenteeism: face-to-face contact is where creativity happens.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier episode on how great minds cluster and multiply each other.
recommendations.reason: Bell Labs, with its corridor of legends, is a textbook example of that thesis.

recommendations.item: Seven Stories That Should Be Films (Episode 23)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Named as one of their favourite episodes, which came about on the fly while shooting in person.
recommendations.reason: Evidence that in-person energy produces their best work.

recommendations.item: Math Is Better Than the Brigadier's Girlfriend (Episode 15)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Another unplanned episode that came out of face-to-face conversation.
recommendations.reason: Same point: creativity comes from being in the same room.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay jokes that the junk-PDP-7 origin of Unix 'runs contrary to any declutter manifesto'. He later notes that decluttered old computers can be revived with Unix.
recommendations.reason: A playful counterpoint: the clutter in an office can sometimes become the next breakthrough.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay brings up his book with Kelkar when praising Bell Labs' culture of improving each other's writing.
recommendations.reason: Ajay uses it as an example of how hundreds of people shaped a book credited to two authors.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions teaching his writing course while asking whether programming makes you a better thinker. The show notes say registration for the February 2024 cohort closes on release day.
recommendations.reason: The course is built on the idea that clear writing and clear thinking reinforce each other in both directions.

core_ideas.concept: The Magic Is Culture, Not Money
core_ideas.explanation: Many labs have had similar budgets and talent without similar results. What set Bell Labs apart was its post-war American optimism and freedom: bosses didn't oppress, staff didn't accept too much top-down authority, and the federated, self-organising management left room to play. Ajay contrasts this with a Stalinist, top-down organisation, and sees the same spirit later in Berkeley's counterculture.
core_ideas.quote: So it's not the magic of resourcing. It is some other magic. It's a magic of culture, it's a magic of management

core_ideas.explanation: Bell Labs welcomed unconventional people and gave them long horizons, but it expected their ideas to turn into real things. Freedom combined with an expectation of eventual usefulness is what made it productive rather than just pleasant.
core_ideas.quote: it was a place for eccentrics but not dreamers.

core_ideas.explanation: Kernighan's lesson from Bell Labs: being physically near great people, through corridors, lunches and watercoolers, multiplies creativity. A flat, collegial structure where nobody's career hung on one boss amplified the effect. Amit uses it to push back on work-from-home as dogma.
core_ideas.quote: there is a striking thing that Kernighan says, which is geography is destiny.

core_ideas.explanation: A first system is built by a few scared mavericks, so it tends to be spare and coherent. Once it succeeds, the second system attracts power-seekers and a long list of feature requests that are hard to refuse, while its builders lose their humility, and it bloats and fails. CTSS was the first system; Multics was the bloated second. Amit's version is that Multics tried to climb many trees at once.
core_ideas.quote: When they were doing the first system they were more human, they were frail, they were terrified, they were quaking in their boots.

core_ideas.explanation: Creative people always work under constraints. Unix came from junk hardware, no budget and a borrowed typesetting brief. Ajay tells Indians in under-resourced organisations that many of their chains are in the mind: C.R. Rao had no 'right to win' and won anyway. Ease the constraints where you can, but don't whine about them.
core_ideas.quote: Or we can dance anyway, even if these chains are there, we can dance anyway.

core_ideas.concept: Engineering and Philosophy Sit on One Shelf
core_ideas.explanation: Culture, aesthetics and philosophy are not separate from science and engineering. Examples include the link between The Elements of Style and The Elements of Programming Style, and the influence of typography on Steve Jobs. Ajay argues that India's split between the doctor-engineer world and the humanities has drained engineering of a sense of what good engineering is.
core_ideas.quote: if you think the words culture and philosophy sit in a different shelf from the words engineering or science, then, you know, I would like to question that.

core_ideas.concept: Simplicity and Beauty as the Mind's Interface
core_ideas.explanation: Systems built from a few simple components, with many features thrown away, work better because people can understand them. Ajay cites David Gelernter's line that when faced with complexity, our only defence is beauty.
core_ideas.quote: I want to use the idea that simplicity and beauty is the user interface of the human mind.

core_ideas.explanation: Build one small tool at a time that does one thing, test it heavily and make it fast, then make it easy to combine tools like Lego, rather than designing a giant enterprise system top-down. Ajay works the same way. He keeps a problem in his head for a long time before coding, picks out the two or three hardest components, solves them with tunnel-vision focus, and only then zooms out to watch the whole design come together.
core_ideas.quote: So build one small tool at a time with limited functionality, but then make it bulletproof.

core_ideas.concept: Writing, Thinking and Programming Are One
core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues clear writing and clear thinking feed each other, citing Deirdre McCloskey (writing is part of research) and Joan Didion (I don't know what I think till I write it down). Ajay extends this to code: good thinkers make better programmers and good programmers become better thinkers, though grinding out code as a job doesn't count. The Bell Labs culture of terse, precise man pages and slim, well-written books is a large part of why its ideas spread so widely.
core_ideas.quote: Writing code is like writing prose. They're not different.

core_ideas.concept: The Man Page Drives the Program
core_ideas.explanation: Writing good documentation forces clear thinking and invites sharp criticism from readers, which improves the program itself. When the manual starts to look convoluted, that's the moment to cut features.
core_ideas.quote: I've seen many times in history that the man page drives the program.

core_ideas.concept: Tend a Garden of Fifty-Year-Old Trees
core_ideas.explanation: Following Donald Knuth, write code as if explaining it to the person sitting beside you, so it lasts. Knuth went furthest by writing programs as essays that switch into code, with tools that split one file into code for the compiler and English for the typesetter. Most software culture tears down the house and starts over. Unix wins by improving mature code for decades, which takes devotion: play for fifty years.
core_ideas.quote: One of the reasons the Unix community has won is because we are now tending a garden with fifty-year-old trees.

core_ideas.concept: Open Source Is Just Science Continued
core_ideas.explanation: Mathematicians publish proofs, so programmers share code. Ajay sets Bill Gates' manifesto for secret commercial software against Richard Stallman's vision of software as open as physics. Microsoft once earned about 90% of the industry's profits yet produced no new idea, while the open world won with TCP/IP, the internet and Unix. Open code lowers the bar to compete, so the many Unix variants are a feature, not a bug. Amit adds that open sharing is simply another form of voluntary market cooperation.
core_ideas.quote: Today it has a fancy name. It's the open source movement. But actually it's just a continuation of a story that began five hundred years ago.

core_ideas.concept: Unix and the Internet as True Digital Public Goods
core_ideas.explanation: Published source code meets the textbook test of a public good. It is non-rival, because your download doesn't reduce mine, and non-excludable. The US Defense Department funded TCP/IP and AT&T paid the early Unix salaries, but the results went out freely to the whole world. Ajay says this needs neither government control nor nationalism.
core_ideas.quote: There's no government in the picture, there is no coercion in the picture, nobody forced anybody.

core_ideas.explanation: Clever people on weak machines with small budgets spent fifty years refining Unix algorithms, so Unix gets more out of less hardware than well-funded corporate code. Old discarded computers can be put back to useful work with it, and developers in this world are held to a higher standard for algorithms.
core_ideas.quote: there has been a stubborn frugality about the Unix world.

core_ideas.explanation: An operating system or network could easily have been designed as a straitjacket of control. Unix and the internet instead accept a degree of anarchism: anonymous use, encryption, VPNs. Spam is the price, but the alternative is central control by a corporation or government, which Ajay pictures as an iris scan before every email and four rupees per message.
core_ideas.quote: The internet is deeply wired for free, flexible, anonymous use.

core_ideas.concept: The Sausage Factory Is Open to Everyone
core_ideas.explanation: The Linux kernel, the world's most complex piece of code, is built in public by thousands of developers around the world. Anyone can watch, learn and contribute, starting with a bug report or a missing document.
core_ideas.quote: So we can just go look at the sausage factory, we can see what is being done by who and how, and then we can start participating and we can start contributing.

core_ideas.explanation: Keep data in plain text rather than proprietary formats so every tool can read and change it. Then chain small commands so the output of one feeds the next, such as sort into tail, or awk into sort into head, and you can do complex work in a single line.
core_ideas.quote: Because plain text files are the universal language by which all the programs speak to each other and are able to read files, modify files.

core_ideas.explanation: In the Unix world there is no sharp line between user and programmer. Within 15 minutes of command-line use, Ajay has viewers writing real awk code and turning a repeated task into a new command of their own.
core_ideas.quote: that generally we blur the lines between nonprogrammers and programmers.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's personal discipline: lowercase names for files, uppercase for directories and special files like the README, underscores instead of spaces, logical structure, and a README in each directory. He manages files that are thirty to forty years old, and this is the only way his future self can understand them.
core_ideas.quote: We do everything as a battle against the frail human mind.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay praises Amit's preparation: 'This boy is not a Bengali dreamer. Look at the number of books he has read for this one episode… Get off your butt and read some books.' Amit replies: 'don't get off your butt. It's a very comfortable place. God gave you a butt for a reason, right? Actually God gave you a butt for two reasons. Both of which we are sort of indulging in.'
Ajay: 'show me where is the beef, or show me where is the rasgulla?' Amit: 'What you said was firstly anti-national and secondly unhealthy. No rasgullas, too much sugar.'
Ajay, listing devices with CPUs inside: 'inside every smartwatch, bracket, I have a dumb watch.'
On Thompson building Unix from a discarded PDP-7: 'this story runs contrary to any declutter manifesto that you do want to keep your PDP 7s'.

On Hamming's prediction that computation would take over: every grad student learns that 'You may think you're doing biology, you may think you're doing political science. Ghoom phir ke, it's just programming.'

Ajay pictures a WhatsApp uncle who wants an Aadhaar iris scan every time you switch on your phone 'because otherwise terrorists will use phones', in a world where you're 'charged four rupees for each email'.
For the Indian nationalists: 'Nobody called it America Stack, they just called it Unix and the Internet.'
Ajay the free-marketeer, before making a public-goods argument: 'So unaccustomed as I am to questioning some of the fundamentals of how modern capitalism works…'
Bill Gates, asked where he'd go in a time machine: December 1947, Bell Labs, when the transistor was created.
Amit quotes a colourful description of why Multics failed: it 'was trying to climb many trees at the same time.'
Richard Hamming: 'The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.' Hamming also predicted in the early sixties that more than half of Bell Labs' work would become computation.
Joan Didion ('I don't know what I think till I write it down') and Deirdre McCloskey ('writing is a part of research'), cited by Amit to tie clear writing to clear thinking.

Ken Thompson's prophecy, as Ajay recounts it: somewhere in a lab sits a little-used, defunct Cray-1 supercomputer, and the next Ken Thompson will write a space travel game on it and start the next revolution in computing.

C.R. Rao as an obscure graduate student at ISI Calcutta before email, with 'no right to win', who still reached the frontier of statistics. Ajay adds that even inside a concentration camp you can write poetry.
Steve Jobs drew a powerful early impetus from the aesthetics of typesetting and font design.

The 'markup' in HTML traces back to Bell Labs' roff/troff typesetting tools, built for patent applications. Ajay also says the 'directories' (folders) other operating systems adopted were invented in Unix.
Bill Gates' manifesto for secret, commercial software versus Richard Stallman's counter-manifesto for software as open as mathematics and physics, which Ajay places in the mid-1970s.
